Hello all,

Here, in Quebec city, (and mostly in all the cities of the province of
Quebec) when a player strike a deal with an other player, the players
did not break the deal, even when the other player has done is part of
his deal and it can be easy to oust him.

Why we do that ? Because a player that break a deal will lost mostly
if not all hope of have a deal again with other players in the city
and even in the other cities of Quebec since the players are in
contact via the web and the mailling list. To have a reputation for
being a deal breaker here is something that will pursue you for a long
time.

What is the dealing metagame in the others cities ?

And is it different when dealing for split of table ?
(Here, no, but elsewhere, it's maybe different)

Thank you for your help,

Here in DC, it's much the opposite. Everyone breaks deals sometimes and
everyone expects their deals to be broken. Well, everyone SHOULD expect that,
some people are still a bit naive. I won't name anyone in particular but you
know who you are, Colin :).

For the most part, we know when a deal is going to be kept. For instance, if
someone can win by breaking a deal, they're going to break it. I don't fault
them for that. Most of the time, deals are adhered to if they benefit both
players (such as "I'll vote for you if you rescue me"). However, one-sided
deals (such as "don't do anything to me and I won't rush you") are usually
broken at some point because there's no incentive to keep them, you can't win
by not hurting your prey.

I consider this to be a good thing, because it makes us more cunning and
conniving players and makes our games more interesting. Deal making, bluffing,
back-stabbing, and trash talking are big parts of this game, and, in my
opinion, that's what makes it so much fun.

Jason

I was talking about deals that benefit both parties. However, if a situation
dictates that one player must put out first and trust the other NOT to take
a victory point later in consideration for the immediate action, then the
ability to make the deal hinges on whether the second player can be trusted
or not. In your locality, it sounds as if few if any players would keep that
deal and knowing that, no one would even consider entering into such a deal.

> True, but people will usually offer deals that benefit both of us, or at
> least they do here. What are these deals where people are giving away vps?

For instance, a Brujah rush combat deck has a prey with lots of fortitude
but little intercept and an !Malk predator with lots of Kindred Spirits
bleed cards but who is basically at the rush combat deck's mercy. Mr. Rush
can say, "Hey, bleed my prey out for me and I'll lay down for you at the
end of the game. Continue just bleeding me now and I'll destroy you." The
people in your city can't make that deal because no one would trust Mr. Rush
to keep it. However, it would be in both of their interests to do so as
neither the Mr. Rush nor the !Malk player is likely to get the first oust
without doing something like that. It sounds as if people in the original
posters city might be able to do it since they have reputations for keeping
such deals.

> I also think that gaming to gain people's trust, so that they will help you
> more in future games is any more appropriate then being super retaliatory
> when someone screws you. Sure it might give you a reputation where people
> won't sens dep you cross table, but so will kicking people's ass outside the
> game. They are both a form of metagaming that takes away from the each
> individual game.

Metagaming is an unresolved philosophical question in multiplayer gaming and
always has been. It's impossible to eliminate no matter what you do. Your
reputation in certain respects will unquestionably affect how players in later
games behave towards you. The only issue is how far one will go to create the
reputation they want to bring to the table. "Kicking people's asses outside
the game" might well be illegal and/or immoral depending on what you're talking
about. Hauling grudges from one game to the next will negatively affect future
gaming and thus (IMO) is self-defeating if the ultimate goal of gaming is to
have fun. However, one DOES have a reputation for how one plays a game whether
one likes it or not. I can certainly understand how players might decide to
tend and nurture that reputation in a positive way, like trees in orchard.

Fred

(don't know if I have such a rep!) and I admit that it's partly pride
that motivates me.

In general I won't offer a deal that I intend to break, or accept one
that I believe either party will break (unless I'm in desperate
straits anyway).

For these reasons it's pretty unlikely that I'll deal with my predator
or prey.

Just about every deal is a once-only affair ("Don't block the Rumours
of Gehenna action and I'll give you an extra master phase action") or
for a specific time (one turn, two turns, whatever). This makes them
much easier to keep without risking the game.

I don't have any personal ill-will towards anyone who breaks a deal,
but if they do so consistency then that does influence decisions.

Tournaments are a different matter. If breaking a deal can get someone
a VP, then by all means they should do so. I consider tournaments to
be different conditions to social play.

Well, that's just your opinion. It is not supported by any game rule. In
fact, AFAICT, there really *isn't* a way to write a rule in a multiplayer
game to avoid such behavior unless you empower a judge to start playing a
player's game for him - which misses the point of having individual players
play. So you need to accept the fact that whether you like it or not,
metagaming is inevitably part of most multiplayer games, the possible

deck will never get by the fortitude deck, ergo 0 VPs - EVER. But he might

much effort, both to delay his eventual demise (i.e., you never know what
might happen if you hang on) and to put some force behind his threat to
do so. Ergo 0 vps for the anti-Malk.

The game win thing doesn't matter either way. They both get VPs WITH the
deal. They neither one of them get a single VP without the deal. Which
is better? It doesn't matter if one or other does or doesn't wind up with
a game win, although I'm sure it would behoove them to negotiate about that
point if they can.

Frankly, you're quibbling here. These situations come up from time whether
you wish to accept it or not.

> I guess I have a game win or bust philosophy.

That's fine. You may, someday, find that you didn't get into the finals of
a tournament for lack of VPs as much as lack of an extra game win, in which
case you might wish to rethink your philosophy. But I'm not trying to
convince you one philosophy or another is better. I'm merely trying to
point out that your's is not the only viable way to look at the situation.

> >

> they aren't playing to win as much as they could be.

To the contrary, the opposite could be said to be true. If you give up a
VP or a game win today but your nobility insures that you're in a much
better position to obtain them in the future, you may well be optimizing
the number of VPs and game wins you get over time. Therefore, if you
doublecross someone today and get a cheap game win, you may very well NOT
be playing to win as much as you could be.

> Nurturing a reputation of someone who will break deals to win, but keep them
> in other cases where the cost is not too high, is a better way to gain vps.

I don't think that can be proved straight out. I think it depends on how the
players you typically play with behave. In some localities, I strongly believe
the opposite could be true.

> It is at least flexible, whereas the honor at all costs philosophy is not.

I'm really confused about what this has to do with flexibility. If you choose
to go for the doublecross in the situation where someone made a deal with you
for prior considerations and are depending on you to keep it when they're
helpless, then you cast your die just as much as someone who inevitably
choose to keep the deal. Your reputation for keeping such deals is hosed so
you have absolutely nothing to gain by keeping them in the future. Basically,
in that situation there's no avoiding the fact that _whatever_ you do is a
permanent thing - so neither choice can be said to be any more flexible than
the other.

By the way, the point of keeping such deals is not "honor at all costs". This
has nothing to do with "honor". It has to do with the practical benefits of
maintaining a reputation for keeping deals when no in-game retribution is
possible.

Fred

Solid premises, but I must disagree with your conclusion. Being trusted
more does not lead to more 'commerce;' you can be the most trusted fellow
at the table, but if you have little to offer, you cannot make deals, but
a fellow who is less trusted, but has large favors to dispense, can
compel dealmaking even in the face of mistrust, because the size of the
favor is worth the risk.

I would argue that, to make the most deals, you need to be the person at
the table with the most 'liquid' resources, where 'liquid' is defined as
'freely directable to another player,' such as Rushing their enemy's
minons, Dementation bleeds at their prey, or vote terms. If you bring
the most to market, you'll make the most transactions.

Here's my thesis, thinking out loud (ie somewhat unexamined):

If it's profitable to make deals in VTES that rely on having "trust
to the point of death", the game is flawed in that respect.

To the extent that cooperation between predator and prey in ousting
other players is rewarded, the basic premise of the game is being
undermined. It's supposed to be an individual game, not a team game.
There were mechanics and incentives devised to try to reduce the
ability and desire of other players to play kingmaker (in a general
sense, not necessarily literally making someone else directly win),
and if they're not strong enough to get people to not do it, the
game design has failed.

In my off-the-top-of-my-head opinion, this game is fun only when
taken seriously (in that all the players are trying to win) but not
*too* seriously (because the multiplayer interference-possibilities
of the game make hyper-competitive play impractical, in my opinion).
Treating deals as sacred because of long-term benefits of having
"a trustworthy reputation" is, to me, taking the game too seriously.

This, to me, seems somewhat questionable. You're making some assumptions
here that I don't think were written down anywhere and therefore are not
going to be assumptions other people make. It is supposed to be an
individual game - but if two people can cooperate to the benefit of both,
why not pursue such a strategy? What seems to be disturbing you is when
cooperation continues absent the single game "yank of the chain", which
either means that the player who holds up his end when he clearly has no
in-game incentive to (any more) must either be doing what he's doing because
of considerations of a later game or due to some other factor such as a
perception of the meaning of "personal honor".

You assert that such things are evidence of failed game design. But that
would assume that a multiplayer game can somehow be designed which would
prevent these considerations from affecting the game, which seems unlikely
to me. There are multiplayer games in which such things have little or no
impact but I think trying to design a game to limit or eliminate them
entirely places huge constraints on how the game can work that it's
probably not worthwhile. The types of game I can think of offhand that
effectively do it (I'm sure there may be others) would be things like
Risk, where player cooperation happens but player victory tends to be a
sudden, runaway sort of thing that no one would knowingly aid once it's
clear it's happening. Or card games where one's abilities to attack or not
attack another's position are so extremely transitory that there's not much
point making deals about them.

The simple point that certain design decisions were made to limit kingmaking
does not imply that dealmaking between players was intended to be verboten in
general. And certainly there's no reason to assume that the designer meant to
eliminate one particular type of deal - in this case a "deal to the death" - as
opposed to any other type such as a deal that would be implicitly understood to
be breakable in the event that no in-game consideration could prevent it.
These are all metagaming questions, not so much game design decisions. Certain
games are more conducive to them then others but I sure wouldn't fault such
games for being badly designed.
